faq.q: Why is biomass smoke a major cause of COPD in East Africa?

exam: A 45‑year‑old woman with chronic cough, night sweats and weight loss presents; what is the next diagnostic step and why? — Obtain sputum for acid‑fast bacilli because TB is most likely in this setting.

A patient with known COPD deteriorates with increased sputum purulence; which two treatments should be started immediately? — Short‑acting β2‑agonist inhaler and oral steroids; add antibiotics if purulent sputum.

You see bilateral crackles and peripheral oedema in a malaria‑positive patient; what complication should you consider and how would you manage it? — Malaria‑related pulmonary oedema; give diuretics and careful fluid balance.

A young adult with wheeze improves after a bronchodilator trial; how do you differentiate asthma from COPD? — Demonstrate reversible airflow obstruction (≥12 % increase in FEV1) and assess exposure history; asthma is reversible, COPD is not.
What red‑flag sign on examination mandates urgent referral for a patient with suspected TB? — Massive haemoptysis (> 200 mL/24 h) or severe hypoxaemia (SpO2 < 85 %).
In a resource‑limited ward without spirometry, how would you stage COPD severity? — Use mMRC dyspnoea scale and WHO performance status together with symptom burden.
Why should macrolide antibiotics be avoided in a patient on rifampicin? — Rifampicin induces hepatic enzymes, reducing macrolide levels and risking treatment failure.

A patient with HIV presents with diffuse bilateral infiltrates and normal chest X‑ray; what is the most likely organism and the key test? — Pneumocystis jirovecii; perform induced sputum or PCR for diagnosis.
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A clinical framework for evaluating common respiratory problems in East African hospitals, focusing on bedside assessment, limited investigations and pragmatic management.

b: Identify acute vs chronic presentation
Determine if the problem is airway, parenchymal, pleural or vascular
sections.p: Respiratory medicine covers diseases affecting the airways and lung parenchyma that cause dyspnoea, cough, sputum or chest pain. Diagnosis starts with a focused history and physical exam, then targeted tests.

b: mMRC 0‑4 correlates with impact on daily life
FEV1 < 50 % predicts higher mortality in COPD
sections.p: Severity is graded by symptom burden, oxygenation and functional limitation. Use the WHO performance status, mMRC dyspnoea scale and, when possible, spirometry (FEV1% predicted).

b: Infectious: TB, bacterial pneumonia, malaria‑related pulmonary oedema
Chronic airway disease: COPD from biomass smoke, asthma, post‑TB bronchiectasis
Cardiogenic: rheumatic heart disease causing pulmonary congestion
Immunocompromised: HIV‑related opportunistic infections (Pneumocystis, Kaposi sarcoma)
Environmental: occupational dust, silica, herbal inhalants
sections.p: In low‑resource East African hospitals the common aetiologies are:

b: Productive cough with night sweats → TB
Wheeze, episodic dyspnoea → asthma
Progressive dyspnoea, barrel chest → COPD
Fever, pleuritic chest pain → bacterial pneumonia
Bilateral crackles, peripheral oedema → heart failure

t.b: What structural abnormality is present? – Shows infiltrates, cavitation, pleural effusion or hyperinflation; if unavailable, rely on clinical pattern and bedside ultrasound.
Is Mycobacterium tuberculosis present? – Positive acid‑fast bacilli confirm TB; if microscopy unavailable, treat empirically when clinical suspicion is high.
What is the oxygen saturation? – < 90 % indicates need for supplemental O₂; if pulse oximeter absent, assess cyanosis and mental status.
What is the airflow limitation? – FEV1/FVC < 0.70 confirms obstructive disease; if unavailable, use symptom scores and exposure history.
Is there leukocytosis or anaemia? – Elevated neutrophils suggest bacterial infection; anaemia worsens dyspnoea.

b: Severe hypoxaemia (SpO2 < 85 %)
Altered mental status or respiratory fatigue
Massive haemoptysis (> 200 mL/24 h)
Tension pneumothorax signs
Rapidly progressive infiltrates in HIV
sections.p: Recognise conditions that need urgent referral or intensive care.

b: TB: standard 6‑month regimen (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol).
Bacterial pneumonia: empiric amoxicillin‑clavulanate or ceftriaxone; avoid macrolides if QT prolongation risk.
COPD exacerbation: short‑acting β2‑agonist inhaler, oral steroids, antibiotics if sputum purulent; give O₂ to keep SpO2 ≥ 90 %.
Asthma acute attack: inhaled rapid‑acting β2‑agonist + systemic steroids; avoid high‑dose β‑blockers.
Heart‑failure pulmonary oedema: loop diuretic, low‑dose ACE inhibitor; avoid NSAIDs.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care.

b: TB: sputum check at 2 months, complete therapy.
COPD: smoking cessation, clean‑fuel stoves, vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal).
Asthma: inhaler technique check, trigger avoidance, written action plan.
sections.p: Arrange review based on diagnosis and severity.

b: Pulmonary TB vs lung cancer – both cause chronic cough and weight loss; cancer rare in young patients without smoking history.
COPD vs asthma – both obstructive; asthma shows reversible airflow obstruction and eosinophilia.
Pneumonia vs pulmonary embolism – both cause pleuritic pain; embolism often has sudden onset and normal chest X‑ray.
sections.p: Conditions that mimic common respiratory presentations.

b: Normal chest X‑ray early TB – rely on sputum and clinical risk.
Pulse oximetry may read falsely high in severe anaemia.
Spirometry over‑estimates obstruction if patient cannot perform forced manoeuvre.
